items.stem: Which term describes the roles played by husbands and wives (or partners) within a marriage or relationship?
items.answer: Conjugal roles
items.markingKey: Conjugal roles: the roles played by husbands and wives (or partners) within a marriage or relationship. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “domestic division of labour”, and give one example.
items.answer: The way housework, childcare and other domestic tasks are divided between members of a household. Example: the woman doing most of the cooking while the man does repairs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the way housework, childcare and other domestic tasks are divided between members of a household); 1 mark for a relevant example such as the woman doing most of the cooking while the man does repairs. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “symmetrical family” and “emotion work”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Symmetrical family: Young and Willmott’s term for a family in which partners’ roles are similar, though not identical (e.g. both partners working and sharing housework). Emotion work: the work of managing the feelings of family members and maintaining relationships (e.g. remembering birthdays and comforting upset children).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Chloe and her husband both work full-time in Singapore; she does the cooking, cleaning and organises the children’s activities, while he does “jobs around the house” at weekends. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: there has been gradual progress towards equality, as men do more domestic work (Gershuny’s lagged adaptation), but further change in attitudes and policies is needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Lina and her husband both work full-time in Doha; she does the cooking, cleaning and organises the children’s activities, while he does “jobs around the house” at weekends. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: roles have become more joint and symmetrical as the family adapts to women’s employment; complementary roles help the family function (Young and Willmott, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A couple in Accra split all housework equally using a shared app, and both work part-time to share childcare. Explain how liberal feminist and radical feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: there has been gradual progress towards equality, as men do more domestic work (Gershuny’s lagged adaptation), but further change in attitudes and policies is needed. Radical feminism: little has changed: women still do most domestic and emotional work, a triple shift that benefits men under patriarchy (Duncombe and Marsden, Delphy and Leonard).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Manila wants to research the division of housework in dual-earner couples in Jakarta. Evaluate the use of semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: interviewer bias may still affect answers; follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the division of housework in dual-earner couples in Jakarta but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are for studying who does the emotion work in families.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they may be the only source of evidence about the past. Limitations: they are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying who does the emotion work in families but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Define the term “joint conjugal roles”.
items.answer: Roles in which partners share tasks, decision-making and leisure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: roles in which partners share tasks, decision-making and leisure. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “segregated conjugal roles” and “conjugal roles”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Segregated conjugal roles: roles in which partners have separate, clearly different tasks and leisure (e.g. a male breadwinner and a female housewife with separate friends). Conjugal roles: the roles played by husbands and wives (or partners) within a marriage or relationship (e.g. who earns, cooks, cleans and cares for children).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Kwame is planning a study of who does the emotion work in families. Explain one limitation of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of who does the emotion work in families. [2]

items.stem: A study of 500 dual-earner couples in Santiago recorded the average weekly hours spent on domestic tasks. Table: average hours per week spent on each task | Men | Women. Cooking | 4 h | 10 h. Cleaning | 2 h | 8 h. Childcare | 8 h | 14 h. (a) Calculate the difference between Cooking and Cleaning for Men and for Women, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that conjugal roles have become symmetrical.
items.answer: (a) Men: 2 hours; Women: 2 hours; the difference is the same for both. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Women than for Men among Cooking, Cleaning, Childcare; Childcare had the highest figure for Women. Gender socialisation leads women to take responsibility for domestic tasks. Qualifications: Women still do more of every task in the table; diaries may be completed inaccurately; tasks such as emotion work are not shown. The data also come from personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) of 500 dual-earner couples in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (2 and 2); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes physical, emotional, sexual or financial abuse between partners or family members?
items.answer: Domestic violence
items.markingKey: Domestic violence: physical, emotional, sexual or financial abuse between partners or family members. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “domestic violence”, and give one example.
items.answer: Physical, emotional, sexual or financial abuse between partners or family members. Example: a partner repeatedly hitting or controlling the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (physical, emotional, sexual or financial abuse between partners or family members); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a partner repeatedly hitting or controlling the other. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “allowance system” and “pooling”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Allowance system: a way of managing money in which one partner (usually the man) gives the other an allowance for household spending (e.g. a husband giving his wife a weekly amount for food). Pooling: a way of managing money in which both partners have access to income and take joint responsibility for spending (e.g. a joint bank account).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A woman in Dubai says her partner checks her phone, controls all the money and stops her seeing her friends, although he has never hit her. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: violence and control are expressions of patriarchy: men use money, decision-making and violence to maintain power over women (Dobash and Dobash, Edgell).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A woman in Cairo says her partner checks her phone, controls all the money and stops her seeing her friends, although he has never hit her. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: inequality and stress caused by low income and insecure work damage relationships and increase violence (Wilkinson); power in families mirrors economic power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of unstructured interviews for studying how couples make financial decisions.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how couples make financial decisions but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “allowance system”.
items.answer: A way of managing money in which one partner (usually the man) gives the other an allowance for household spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a way of managing money in which one partner (usually the man) gives the other an allowance for household spending. [1]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of financial decision-making in couples (600 couples, Toronto). Table: percentage of couples saying major financial decisions are made | 2000 | 2025. Mainly the man | 40% | 26%. Mainly the woman | 16% | 14%. Jointly | 44% | 60%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Jointly change between 2000 and 2025?
items.answer: +16 percentage points
items.markingKey: 60 − 44 = +16 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A survey of 600 couples in Nairobi produced the data below. Table: percentage of couples saying major financial decisions are made | 2000 | 2025. Mainly the man | 38% | 24%. Mainly the woman | 16% | 14%. Jointly | 46% | 62%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Mainly the man between 2000 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that decision-making power in couples has become equal.
items.answer: (a) (24 − 38) ÷ 38 × 100 = -36.8%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Jointly; the figure fell for Mainly the man, Mainly the woman; Jointly had the highest figure for 2025. Women’s rising income gives them more say (resource theory). Qualifications: Men still make more decisions alone than women; joint decisions may hide unequal influence; answers in interviews may be socially desirable. The data also come from structured interviews of 600 couples in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (24 − 38) ÷ 38 × 100; 1 mark for -36.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.answer: Child-centred family

items.stem: What is meant by the term “age patriarchy”? Give one example.
items.answer: Gittins’s term for adult domination over children. Example: parents controlling what children wear and where they go.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Gittins’s term for adult domination over children); 1 mark for a relevant example such as parents controlling what children wear and where they go. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “infant mortality rate” and “age patriarchy”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Infant mortality rate: the number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1,000 live births (e.g. 4 infant deaths per 1,000 live births). Age patriarchy: Gittins’s term for adult domination over children (e.g. parents controlling what children wear and where they go).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a rural area near Jakarta, many 12-year-olds leave school to work on family farms. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: children’s experiences depend on class: poorer children have worse health, education and opportunities, while childhood is also commercialised by capitalism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a rural area near Manila, many 12-year-olds leave school to work on family farms. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: children, like women, experience age patriarchy: adults control their lives, and the dark side includes abuse (Gittins).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research children’s use of digital technology.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: only small samples can be studied, so results are difficult to generalise; the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying children’s use of digital technology but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Distinguish between “infant mortality rate” and “helicopter parenting”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Infant mortality rate: the number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1,000 live births (e.g. 4 infant deaths per 1,000 live births). Helicopter parenting: a style of parenting in which parents closely supervise and control children’s activities (e.g. parents not allowing children to play outside alone).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a rural area near Kuala Lumpur, many 12-year-olds leave school to work on family farms. Explain how Marxist and radical feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: children’s experiences depend on class: poorer children have worse health, education and opportunities, while childhood is also commercialised by capitalism. Radical feminism: children, like women, experience age patriarchy: adults control their lives, and the dark side includes abuse (Gittins).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “beanpole family”, and give one example.
items.answer: A multi-generational family that is long and thin, with several generations but few members in each. Example: great-grandparents, grandparents, parents and one child.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a multi-generational family that is long and thin, with several generations but few members in each); 1 mark for a relevant example such as great-grandparents, grandparents, parents and one child. [2]

items.stem: In Manila, many grandparents collect their grandchildren from school every day while both parents work. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: later life is increasingly varied and chosen; older people construct diverse identities and relationships.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Noah, a sociology student, is designing a project on the role of grandparents in childcare. Explain one strength and one limitation of using official statistics for this study.
items.answer: Strength: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect. Limitation: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of the role of grandparents in childcare. [4]

items.stem: Grace, aged 52, lives in Hanoi and looks after her 80-year-old father while also supporting her two teenagers. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: families adapt to demographic change: beanpole families and grandparents provide vital support such as childcare and care for the elderly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes roles in which partners have separate, clearly different tasks and leisure?
items.answer: Segregated conjugal roles
items.markingKey: Segregated conjugal roles: roles in which partners have separate, clearly different tasks and leisure. [1]

items.stem: State one reason why women still do more housework than men in many families.
items.answer: Women do more emotion work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. women do more emotion work. [1]

items.stem: Explain Duncombe and Marsden’s argument that women perform a triple shift of paid work, domestic work and emotion work, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Duncombe and Marsden found women did most of the emotional work of maintaining family relationships. Criticism: Some argue men also do emotional work that is less visible.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Radical feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: +3 hours

items.stem: Time-use diaries kept by 400 dual-earner couples in Nairobi produced the following data. Table: average hours per week spent on each task | Men | Women. Cooking | 5 h | 8 h. Cleaning | 3 h | 8 h. Childcare | 5 h | 13 h. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for Women. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) Childcare (13 h). (b) The figure is higher for Women than for Men among Cooking, Cleaning, Childcare; Childcare had the highest figure for Women.

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Cape Town. “A study in Mumbai used questionnaires with 600 couples. 72% of men said they “shared housework equally” with their partner, but only 41% of women in the same couples agreed. Couples where the woman earned more than the man were most likely to report sharing.” (a) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying conjugal roles. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the domestic division of labour is now equal in most couples.
items.answer: (a) Closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. (b) For: Many respondents report sharing, and Young and Willmott and Gershuny suggest roles are becoming more joint, especially where women have economic power. Against: The gap between men’s and women’s answers suggests social desirability and lack of validity; feminist studies (Oakley, Duncombe and Marsden) show women still do more, including emotion work. Also consider how far a single study using self-completion questionnaires can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research who does the emotion work in families. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying who does the emotion work in families but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.answer: 1. Respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script. 2. The fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why domestic violence is difficult to measure.
items.answer: Under-reporting by victims (fear, shame, dependence); police recording practices; hidden coercive control; changing definitions; victim surveys depend on disclosure; the dark figure.

items.stem: Mohammed, a sociology student, is designing a project on children’s use of digital technology. Evaluate the use of non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability. Limitations: the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying children’s use of digital technology but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why conjugal roles may have become more joint.
items.answer: Women’s employment and income (resources theory); changing gender norms; commercialisation of housework; new technology; geographical mobility and privatised families (Young and Willmott); legal changes such as parental leave.

Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Women’s employment and income (resources theory); changing gender norms; commercialisation of housework; new technology; geographical mobility and privatised families (Young and Willmott); legal changes such as parental leave. items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, is designing a project on the division of housework in dual-earner couples in Jakarta. Evaluate the use of non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability; it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. Limitations: private behaviour in the home is rarely open to observation; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the division of housework in dual-earner couples in Jakarta but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes a way of managing money in which both partners have access to income and take joint responsibility for spending?
items.answer: Pooling
items.markingKey: Pooling: a way of managing money in which both partners have access to income and take joint responsibility for spending. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Dobash and Dobash’s view that domestic violence is linked to men’s attempts to assert authority over their wives.
items.answer: They found violent incidents were often set off by what husbands saw as challenges to their authority, such as questioning about money.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: They found violent incidents were often set off by what husbands saw as challenges to their authority, such as questioning about money. [2]

items.stem: Jonas earns twice as much as his wife in Singapore and insists on deciding where the family goes on holiday and which school the children attend. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: inequality and stress caused by low income and insecure work damage relationships and increase violence (Wilkinson); power in families mirrors economic power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A woman in Bangkok says her partner checks her phone, controls all the money and stops her seeing her friends, although he has never hit her. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: inequality and stress caused by low income and insecure work damage relationships and increase violence (Wilkinson); power in families mirrors economic power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Hana, a sociology student, is designing a project on domestic violence in Kuala Lumpur. Evaluate the use of covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it may be the only way to study a group that hides its activities from outsiders; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: secretly recording sensitive behaviour without consent raises serious ethical problems of deception and harm; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying domestic violence in Kuala Lumpur but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that children’s position has steadily improved and they are now better cared for and protected?
items.answer: March of progress view
items.markingKey: March of progress view: the view that children’s position has steadily improved and they are now better cared for and protected. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which adults control children.
items.answer: Control over time (bedtimes, routines); control over space (where they can go); control over bodies (dress, touch); economic dependency; restrictions on access to resources (Hockey and James).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: In a rural area near Kathmandu, many 12-year-olds leave school to work on family farms. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: childhood is fluid and changing; media and technology blur the line between adult and child (Postman).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Parents in Lisbon drive their children to school, organise their after-school activities and track their phones. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: the march of progress view: children are better cared for, protected and educated than in the past, and families are more child-centred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying children’s use of digital technology.
items.answer: Strengths: because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided; it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity. Limitations: studying children covertly is ethically unacceptable because they cannot consent and are vulnerable; the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying children’s use of digital technology but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).

Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: State one effect of an ageing population on family life.
items.answer: More care for elderly relatives, often by women.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. more care for elderly relatives, often by women. [1]

items.stem: Explain Hunt’s argument that older people’s experiences are increasingly shaped by individual choices rather than fixed stages of life, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Hunt argued that life-course stages are blurred and that older people choose varied lifestyles. Criticism: Poverty, ill health and ageism limit choice for many older people.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Postmodernism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: In Nairobi, many grandparents collect their grandchildren from school every day while both parents work. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: families adapt to demographic change: beanpole families and grandparents provide vital support such as childcare and care for the elderly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]
